newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Who's Who in Zaire's crisis.
newsitem.headline: Who's Who in Zaire's crisis.

text.p: Zaire, a sprawling giant at the heart of Africa, has a wealth of minerals and other natural advantages.
It is a nation which many outsiders -- not least Belgium's 19th century coloniser King Leopold -- believed or believe should be one of the continent's richest.
Here are thumb-nail sketches of some of the main players as a Tutsi-led revolt from the east threatens to break veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko's hold over its destiny.
PRESIDENT MOBUTU SESE SEKO

Zaire's strongman for over three decades, Mobutu, 66, has spent most of his time in Europe since cancer surgery there in August. He seized power in a 1965 coup and has ruled ever since with guile and cunning, amassing a fortune but drawing fire from critics for human rights abuses. He embraced democratic reforms in 1990 under intense foreign and domestic pressure. Multi-party elections have been repeatedly postponed.
LAURENT KABILA

A veteran Mobutu foe, Kabila, 56, heads the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL). A former Marxist, he is from mineral-rich Shaba Province. His forces have notched up victory after victory and now hold one fifth of Zaire. He was a supporter of slain independence prime minister Patrice Lumumba, a nationalist with Marxist leanings.
KENGO WA DONDO

Kengo, a wealthy businessman, is Zaire's half-Polish and part-Rwandan Tutsi prime minister. A prime minister under Mobutu's one-party system, he took office again in 1994 saying his priority was to clean up Zaire's corruption-plagued economy. A proponent of a military solution to the revolt, he has come in for growing criticism following the army's poor showing.
ETIENNE TSHISEKEDI

Tshisekedi, leader of Zaire's main political opposition, is a veteran opponent of Mobutu. He and his Union for Democracy and Social Progress enjoy widespread support among Kinshasa's poor and urge peace talks with the rebels. A national conference elected Tshisekedi prime minister in 1992 but Mobutu sacked him a year later. He bitterly rejects Kengo's right to the job.
ANTOINE GIZENGA

Another veteran radical and Mobutu foe, Gizenga was a minister in Lumumba's independence government. He adopted Lumumba's mantle after his death and is widely viewed as guardian of the Lumumbist tradition. He heads the Unified Party of Lumumbists.
GENERAL MAHELE LIEKO BOKOUNGO

Named armed forces chief-of-staff with wide-ranging powers in December, Mahele is one of Zaire's few top generals to have distinguished himself on the battlefield. Most owe promotions to family or other links to Mobutu. But Mahele, trained in France and Israel, has said little since the collapse of the much-heralded army counter-offensive in January .
GENERAL NZIMBI NGBALE

Nzimbi, who has close family ties to Mobutu, commands the Special Presidential Division, the most disciplined, best-paid and professional of Zaire's fighting forces. Their duty is to ensure Mobutu's personal security and defend vital national interests.
GENERAL ELUKI MONGA AUNDU

Eluki is an outspoken former army chief-of-staff from the same Equateur region as Mobutu. He was sacked from the job in November after accusing the government of failing to provide the means to fight the rebels.
HONORE NGBANDA NZAMBO
Ngbanda is Mobutu's security advisor. A former intelligence chief and minister of defence, he represented Zaire in South Africa during an attempt by President Nelson Mandela to mediate in February.
ARCHBISHOP LAURENT MONSENGWO PASINYA
The Roman Catholic Archbishop of Zaire's third city of Kisangani, Monsengwo was head of Zaire's transitional parliament but resigned in 1995.
KAMANDA WA KAMANDA
Kamanda is Zaire's foreign minister. A career politician and a former assistant secretary general of the Organisation of African Unity, he is currently a centrist allied with Kengo.
BEMBA SAOLONA
Millionaire businessman and a Mobutu supporter in the interim parliament. He has called for talks with the rebels.
